record.original_question: For N = {1,2,...,n}, determine the largest subset of N with the property that no m elements of the subset form an arithmetic progression, and ask the analogous question when geometric progressions are forbidden instead. More generally, for a given m-ary relation R on a set N, determine the largest subset whose m-element subsets never satisfy R, including the case where N is infinite such as an interval of real numbers.

evidence.quote: Find the maxim number of elements extracted from N such that any m from these be not an arithmetic progression ... Same question when the m elements must not be a geometrical progression. More generally: Let R be a given m - ary relation on a field N.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let n and m ≥ 3 be positive integers, and let N = {1, 2, ..., n}.

(a) Determine the maximum cardinality r_m(n) of a subset S ⊆ N such that no m distinct elements of S form an arithmetic progression (i.e., S contains no m-term arithmetic progression). Provide sharp upper and lower bounds, and the asymptotic behavior of r_m(n) as n → ∞.

(b) Determine the analogous maximum g_m(n), where instead one forbids m distinct elements of S from forming a geometric progression (i.e., no m-term geometric progression a, ar, ar^2, ..., ar^{m−1} of positive rationals/integers).

(c) More generally, let N be an arbitrary set (possibly infinite, for example an interval of real numbers), and let R be a given m-ary relation on N. Determine (or estimate) the maximum cardinality, or supremum size, of a subset S ⊆ N such that no m-tuple of distinct elements of S satisfies R. Specialize the answer to natural cases such as R = "is an arithmetic progression" or R = "is a geometric progression" when N is an interval of real numbers.
artifact.status_search_result: The arithmetic-progression case (a) is the classical problem behind Szemerédi's theorem (1975), which shows r_m(n) = o(n) for every m ≥ 3. Quantitative bounds are still being improved: Kelley–Meka (2023) gave near-optimal bounds for m = 3, and Leng–Sah–Sawhney (2024) proved r_m(n) ≪ n · exp(−(log log n)^{c_m}) for m ≥ 5. So exact values and tight asymptotics remain open in general. The geometric-progression variant has elementary bounds (since {a_i} is geometric iff {log a_i} is arithmetic, reducing it to the arithmetic case after passing to exponents of primes), and explicit constructions are known but the optimal density is also open. The fully general m-ary relation question is a meta-problem with no single answer; it subsumes many open extremal problems.

status_evidence.title: Szemerédi's theorem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Szemerédi's theorem states that for every k and every positive density delta, sufficiently large N guarantee a k-term AP.
status_evidence.claim: Existence settled (Szemerédi 1975), but precise extremal bounds remain open.

status_evidence.title: Improved Bounds for Szemerédi's Theorem (Leng–Sah–Sawhney, 2024)
status_evidence.snippet: For k ≥ 5, r_k(N) ≪ N exp(−(log log N)^{c_k}).
status_evidence.claim: Recent improvements show the problem is actively studied and quantitative bounds are not tight.

status_evidence.title: Roth's theorem on arithmetic progressions - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Kelley–Meka recently improved the bound for r_3(N).
status_evidence.claim: Even the 3-term case continues to see improvements; optimal constants unresolved.
